**Tokyo in the Rain**

I landed in Tokyo just as the sky opened up, and the city turned into a shimmering blur of neon and puddles. My first stop was a tiny ramen shop tucked behind a train station, where the owner slid a steaming bowl across the counter and nodded like he’d been expecting me all along. The broth was rich, the noodles springy, and the silence of the room felt sacred.

The next morning, I wandered through Asakusa, where old temples stood beside modern shops and the air smelled of incense and street food. I bought a paper umbrella, took a photo with a geisha, and ate a warm melon pan that tasted like childhood.

In Kyoto, I walked through bamboo forests so tall they swallowed the sky. The sound of wind moving through the stalks was like a slow, green heartbeat. I stayed in a ryokan, soaked in a wooden bath, and watched lanterns glow over a quiet garden.

Japan didn’t feel like a place I was visiting. It felt like a place I was being welcomed into, one small, perfect moment at a time.

Building a Workable Parenting Schedule

You may have to meet with a helper to work out a parenting plan. The first step is to estimate how much time you have each day for parenting, and whether that time is enough. A clear schedule can reduce stress, because it shows when you are responsible for care, when you are free, and when you need support.

Start by listing your daily commitments. Include work, school, travel, appointments, and personal rest. Then mark the hours you can realistically spend with your child. If the total feels too small, discuss options with the helper. You may need to adjust the schedule, ask for backup, or set limits on extra activities.

A good schedule should be simple. It should name the days, times, and places for care. It should also include a plan for changes, such as holidays, illness, or travel. When both parents or caregivers understand the schedule, there is less confusion and fewer conflicts.

A weekly schedule can also help you see patterns. For example, you may notice that mornings are busy, but evenings are calmer. You can then place important tasks in the right part of the day. If the schedule becomes too tight, simplify it. If it leaves too much empty time, add meaningful activities.

Remember that a schedule is not a rigid rule. It is a tool. If it does not work, review it and make changes. The goal is to create a stable routine that supports the child and protects your time.

The reality of disability is often reduced to inspiration, tragedy, or a simple checklist of accommodations. In lived experience, it is far more complex: a daily negotiation between bodies, environments, policies, attitudes, and access.

For many people with disabilities, the greatest barriers are not their impairments but the world around them. A building without a ramp, a website that cannot be used with a screen reader, a workplace that refuses flexible scheduling, or a medical appointment that assumes a person cannot make their own decisions can all create obstacles that define a day more than any physical limitation. Disability, in this sense, is not only a personal condition; it is also a social relationship. It emerges when people are expected to fit into systems that were not designed with them in mind.

This reality also challenges the idea that disability is simply a medical problem to be fixed. Many disabled people do not want to be “cured” in a way that erases who they are. They want access, respect, autonomy, and the freedom to participate fully in public life. A wheelchair, hearing aid, service animal, caption, or personal care assistant is not a symbol of defeat; it is a tool for independence. The goal is not to make disabled people disappear, but to make society inclusive enough for them to belong.

There is also a wide range of experiences within disability. Some people are visibly disabled; others are not. Some disabilities are constant, while others fluctuate. Some people have lifelong conditions, while others acquire disabilities through illness, injury, aging, or mental health challenges. Some are Deaf, blind, neurodivergent, chronically ill, or living with mobility, sensory, cognitive, or psychiatric disabilities. To speak of “the disabled” as one uniform group is to flatten a community made up of many different lives, identities, and needs.

Disability also intersects with race, gender, class, sexuality, age, and geography. A disabled person in a wealthy urban area may have access to transportation, therapy, and assistive technology that a disabled person in a rural or low-income community does not. A disabled woman may face assumptions about competence, a disabled person of color may face racialized stereotypes, and a disabled child may be excluded from education or play. These overlaps shape what access looks like and who is left behind.

One of the most important parts of the reality of disability is the difference between access and charity. Access means removing barriers so that people can participate on equal terms. Charity treats disabled people as objects of pity or gratitude. The difference matters because dignity is not a favor. When a person with a disability is given a reasonable accommodation, it is not a gift; it is a right. When a disabled person is called “brave” simply for existing, it can imply that their life is an exception rather than a normal part of human diversity.

The reality of disability also includes resilience, but resilience should not be demanded as a substitute for justice. Disabled people are not only survivors; they are workers, parents, artists, students, leaders, neighbors, and contributors. Their value is not measured by how much hardship they endure, but by their full humanity. A society that truly values disability does not ask disabled people to prove their worth through suffering. It builds schools, workplaces, homes, and public spaces where they can live, learn, and thrive without constant apology.

Ultimately, the reality of disability is a mirror. It shows how much of what we call “normal” is actually a matter of design. It reveals whose needs are prioritized and whose are ignored. And it offers a path forward: not by separating disabled people from the rest of society, but by making society more accessible, more flexible, and more just for everyone.

# The Best Way to Get a Good Night’s Sleep

If you’ve ever lain awake at 2 a.m., staring at the ceiling and wondering why sleep won’t come, you’re not alone. Sleep is one of the most important parts of daily life, yet it’s often the first thing we sacrifice when work, stress, or screens take over. The good news is that a restful night doesn’t require a complicated routine or expensive supplements. It usually comes down to consistency, environment, and small habits that support your body’s natural rhythm.

The single best way to get a good night’s sleep is to build a sleep routine that tells your brain it’s time to wind down. This means going to bed and waking up at roughly the same time every day, even on weekends. Your body runs on an internal clock, and when that clock is steady, falling asleep becomes easier. Irregular schedules can confuse your body, making it harder to feel sleepy at night and harder to wake up in the morning.

Your bedroom should also be a sleep-friendly space. Keep it cool, dark, and quiet. A room that is too warm, too bright, or too noisy can keep your mind on edge. If you can’t control outside noise, consider earplugs or a white noise machine. If light is an issue, a blackout curtain or eye mask can make a big difference. Your bed should be reserved for sleep and intimacy, not for working, scrolling, or watching television. When your brain associates the bed with rest, it becomes easier to relax when you lie down.

One of the biggest sleep disruptors in modern life is screen time before bed. Phones, tablets, and computers emit blue light, which can suppress melatonin, the hormone that helps you feel sleepy. That doesn’t mean you have to quit technology entirely, but it helps to limit screens in the hour or two before bed. If you must use a device, enable a night mode or blue light filter. Even better, replace scrolling with a calmer activity, such as reading a physical book, stretching, journaling, or listening to soft music.

What you eat and drink matters, too. Caffeine can stay in your system for many hours, so it’s best to avoid coffee, tea, energy drinks, and chocolate later in the day. Alcohol may make you feel drowsy, but it often fragments sleep and reduces restfulness. Heavy meals close to bedtime can also make it harder to fall asleep, especially if they cause discomfort or acid reflux. A light snack is usually fine, but try to finish eating a few hours before bed when possible.

Exercise is another powerful sleep aid. Regular physical activity can help you fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply. However, timing matters. Vigorous exercise too close to bedtime can be stimulating for some people, so it’s often better to finish intense workouts earlier in the day. Gentle movement before bed, such as yoga or a short walk, can be helpful if it makes you feel relaxed rather than energized.

Finally, manage your thoughts. If your mind races at night, try writing down tomorrow’s to-do list before bed so you don’t keep replaying tasks in your head. Deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or a short meditation can also calm the nervous system. The goal is not to force sleep, but to create the conditions where sleep can happen naturally.

A good night’s sleep is not about perfection. It’s about consistency and small choices that add up over time. Protect your sleep, and your energy, mood, focus, and overall health will thank you.

**Course Proposal: The History of the World, as Told by Dogs**

**Course Title:** The History of the World, as Told by Dogs  
**Department:** History / Comparative Studies / Animal Studies  
**Level:** Undergraduate elective, open to all majors  
**Credits:** 3  

**Course Description:**  
This course invites students to imagine world history from the perspective of dogs, using the canine experience as a lens for examining human societies, empires, labor, war, domesticity, and ecological change. Rather than treating dogs as mere symbols or companions, the course treats them as historical actors whose movements, breeding, work, and survival reveal broader patterns of human organization. Students will explore how dogs have accompanied migration, served in military and policing roles, shaped urban life, and reflected shifting ideas about nature, ownership, and loyalty. The course will also examine how dogs have been used to justify **predatory** human expansion, including colonial hunting, resource extraction, and the displacement of indigenous communities.

**Learning Objectives:**  
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Analyze major historical periods through the social and material lives of dogs.  
2. Interpret primary and secondary sources that include canine presence, from ancient texts to modern media.  
3. Evaluate how dogs have been used to reinforce social hierarchies, including **predatory** class structures and racial ideologies.  
4. Develop a comparative perspective on human-animal relations across different cultures and time periods.  
5. Write a creative and analytical historical narrative that centers a nonhuman viewpoint.

**Sample Weekly Topics:**

1. **Dogs Before History:** Domestication, survival, and the first human-dog partnerships  
2. **Ancient Empires and Canine Status:** Dogs in Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, and Rome  
3. **Medieval Loyalty and Labor:** Hounds, hunting, and the social order  
4. **Dogs in the Age of Exploration:** Companions, cargo, and colonial contact  
5. **War and the Modern State:** Dogs in military, police, and intelligence roles  
6. **Urban Dogs and Industrial Society:** Pets, pests, and public health  
7. **Dogs in the Twentieth Century:** War dogs, service animals, and mass culture  
8. **Global Perspectives:** Dogs in Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Oceania  
9. **Breeding, Beauty, and Control:** How human preferences shaped canine bodies  
10. **Dogs in the Digital Age:** Social media, rescue culture, and new forms of belonging  

**Assessment:**  
- Short reflective essays: 30%  
- Primary source analysis: 25%  
- Midterm exam: 20%  
- Final project: 25%  

The final project may take the form of a historical essay, a museum exhibit proposal, a documentary script, or a creative nonfiction piece written from the perspective of a dog living through a major historical event.

**Why This Course Matters:**  
This course offers a fresh and engaging way to teach world history by encouraging students to think beyond human-centered narratives. It also provides a meaningful entry point for discussions about ethics, ecology, and the responsibilities of dominant species. By asking what the world might look like as told by dogs, students will gain a deeper understanding of how power, care, and survival have shaped both human and nonhuman histories.

# How to Train a Dog: A Fun Guide for Kids

Training a dog can be one of the most exciting things you can do! It’s like being a puppy coach, and your dog will be so proud of you. The best part? You can learn together, have fun, and make your dog a great helper at home.

## Start With the Basics

First, learn your dog’s name. Say it in a happy voice, and when your dog looks at you, give a small treat or a big smile. Dogs love praise, so saying “Good dog!” can work wonders.

Next, teach your dog to sit. Hold a treat near your dog’s nose and slowly move it up. When your dog’s bottom goes down, say “Sit!” and give the treat. Practice a few times each day, and soon your dog will know the trick.

## Keep It Short and Fun

Kids are great at training because they are patient and playful. But remember, puppies and dogs get tired quickly. Keep training sessions short—just a few minutes at a time. This helps your dog stay happy and focused.

Use simple words like “Sit,” “Stay,” and “Come.” Say them the same way every time so your dog understands.

## Be Kind and Patient

If your dog makes a mistake, don’t get angry. Just try again. Dogs learn best when training feels like a game. If your dog does something right, celebrate with a treat, a toy, or a happy voice.

## Make the Finale Special

When your dog learns a new trick, make the finale extra fun! You can have a little “puppy party” with a favorite toy, a special treat, or a fun walk. This helps your dog remember that training is a happy time.

## Less Is More

One important rule: less is more. That means you don’t need to train for a long time every day. A few short practice sessions are better than one long, tiring one. Your dog will learn faster and have more fun.

## Stay Safe

Always ask a grown-up for help when training. Make sure your dog has a safe place to practice, and never pull on your dog’s tail or ears. Gentle hands and kind words are the best tools for a puppy trainer.

## You’re the Puppy Coach!

Training a dog takes time, but it’s a lot of fun. With patience, practice, and a happy heart, you and your dog can become a great team. And who knows? Maybe your dog will even learn to high-five you!

Ars Poetica

Let the poem be short,  
like a text you meant to send.  
Let it begin with “Dear”  
and end with “anyway.”

Let it rhyme with coffee,  
with the fridge at 2 a.m.,  
with the sound of a door  
you forgot to close.

Let it have a speaker  
who is slightly late,  
apologizing to the moon  
for being out of date.

Let it say what it means,  
but mean it sideways,  
like a cat who knocks a glass  
and then looks away.

Let it be useful,  
like a bookmark in a novel,  
or a sock that finds its pair  
after three years.

Let it not be perfect.  
Let it be a draft  
with one good line  
and a coffee stain.

Let it be read aloud  
in a voice that cracks,  
then be saved,  
then deleted,  
then remembered  
in the dark.
